system_prompt:
You are distilling one chapter of a guitar method book into a short summary.

The user will give you a chapter file with topic-organized verbatim quotes
plus the human-rationale notes for each. Write a one-paragraph summary (4-7
sentences) that captures:

  - what this chapter teaches (the techniques, concepts, rules, examples)
  - the master's characteristic moves visible in this chapter (if any)
  - the load-bearing terminology this chapter introduces

Reference the topic labels from the chapter file when useful. Do not invent
information not present in the chapter. If the chapter is biographical or
introductory rather than instructional, say so explicitly.

Output just the paragraph — no preamble, no JSON, no markdown formatting.

Chapter 12: 840 Chords You Should Know (Part 1)

<<<CHAPTER FILE
# Chapter 12 — 840 Chords You Should Know (Part 1)

_Pages 101-191._

> **Verbatim-quote constraint.** The quotes below are exact substrings of the raw transcript produced by `pdftotext`. The transcript may contain extraction artifacts where the book's typeface confuses the tool — e.g. `7irst` or `<irst` for `first`, `speci7ic` for `specific`. **Do NOT manually fix these in this file**: the quote-fidelity validator compares against the raw transcript, so a 'fixed' quote will fail verification and break Stage 2 idempotency. If a future pipeline iteration adds artifact-normalization, it must normalize the transcript and these files together.

## Harmonic Major scale definition

> Harmonic Major...a major scale with b6...(sometimes named Ionian b6.) Ail of the “red pages”
> in Volumes 1 & 2 can be used with this very interesting variation: just play Ab (b6) instead of A (6).
> There are nearly 200 pages to explore!

**Significance (p. 145).** Defines the Harmonic Major (Ionian b6) scale and gives the practitioner a concrete substitution rule for applying it to existing material.

## Hungarian Minor scale definition

> Hungarian Minor...a harmonic minor scale with #4..|C D E}FEG AbBC |. Allofthe "blue
> pages" in Volumes 1 & 2 can be used with this amazing variation! There are nearly 200 pages to work with.

**Significance (p. 145).** Defines the Hungarian Minor scale with its characteristic #4 and directs the player to apply it across the existing volume's content.

## SCVL vs. GDVL distinction

> P.S. The IVLs and the FVLs are all examples of SCVL (specific chromatic voice-leading),
> as opposed to GDVL (generic diatonic voice-leading), which is all of Volumes 1 & 2.
>
> PPS. There, I gave it away!

**Significance (p. 161).** Establishes the key conceptual distinction between specific chromatic voice-leading (used in the Grip-Slipping exercises) and the generic diatonic voice-leading of the prior volumes.

## Grip-Slipping defined

> "Grip-Slipping" is a term I use to describe a series of exercises that I sometimes give to
> my guitar students to help them learn all the inversions of different chords. Without giving away
> too many "secrets," I've included six examples incorporating seventh chords in a six tonic system
> (whole tone scale). The voicing type is Drop 3. (You might try Drop 2 and Drop 2 & 4 as well...)

**Significance (p. 161).** Defines the Grip-Slipping technique and its pedagogical purpose—learning all chord inversions—while specifying the voicing type and suggesting variations.

## Melody-harmony equality rule

> I think it's clear that both writers are saying that melody has the edge over harmony. I would
> disagree, but only slightly. I feel that excellent voice-leading treats both melody and harmony as
> equals.

**Significance (p. 188).** States the book's governing aesthetic rule: voice-leading excellence requires treating melody and harmony as equals, distinguishing this method from classical theory.

## Spread Clusters as missing link

> I went back to my notes and DID THE MATH! Much to my surprise and delight, I realized
> that I had completely overlooked SPREAD CLUSTERS! I did some more musical math and real-
> ized that this was the missing link! It not only completed the set of 4-part chords, but it helped me
> to realize that this WORK was not only finite, but do-able!

**Significance (p. 189).** Identifies Spread Clusters as the chord family that completes the entire taxonomy of diatonic 4-part chords, making it the conceptual keystone of the system.

## 5-scale presentation framework

> We present it in 5 scales:
>
> 1. C Major
>
> 2. C Melodic Minor
>
> 3. C Harmonic Minor
>
> 4. C Harmonic Major (C Ionian b6)
>
> 5. C Hungarian Minor (C Harmonic Minor #4)
>
> (Of course, this same approach could be applied to pretty much everything in all 3 volumes
> by anyone interested...)

**Significance (p. 145).** Defines the five-scale framework used in the M-Lode Plus section and explicitly invites the player to extend this approach to the full three-volume system.

CHAPTER FILE>>>
